extracted.intended_audience: general readers and people researching television/weekly sketch-comedy production (e.g., students, media researchers, aspiring SNL staff)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and operational standards describing how a weekly Saturday Night Live episode is developed, selected, rehearsed, recorded, broadcast, and archived, plus related staffing and format considerations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekly pitching and writing schedule
rubrics_metrics.description: The host is invited to pitch ideas during the pitch meeting. Tuesday is the only day dedicated purely to writing the scripts; writing may not begin until 8:00 p.m. on Tuesday and usually extends through the night into the following morning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The bulk of the work revolves around pitching ideas during earlier meetings; some sketchwriting may occur on the day of the pitch, but the concentrated writing night is Tuesday starting no earlier than 8:00 p.m.

rubrics_metrics.name: Wednesday read-through meeting
rubrics_metrics.description: At 5:00 p.m. on Wednesday, sketches are read by the cast during a round-table meeting in the writers' room attended by writers, producers, technical experts, and others, resulting in attendance of approximately fifty people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: At the read-through there may be at least forty sketch ideas that are read in turn, with the read-through lasting upwards of three hours; technical experts (e.g., make-up artists) attend because some ideas may require their input.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sketch selection and show breakdown
rubrics_metrics.description: After the read-through, the head writer (Michaels), the guest host, and some producers decide the layout of the show and which sketches will be developed for air. Writers and cast are then shown the show breakdown to learn which sketches survived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Selection is done quickly after read-through; decisions determine which sketches proceed to rewriting and rehearsal. This is the primary gatekeeping moment for sketch advancement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rewriting and rehearsal timeline
rubrics_metrics.description: Sketches may be rewritten starting the same day as the read-through but will certainly commence on Thursday. Rehearsals occur Friday or Saturday, with a rehearsal before a live audience at 8:00 p.m. on Saturday before the live show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sketches scheduled beyond Thursday receive Friday/Saturday rehearsals; sketches that make it to the live rehearsal may still be removed, often leaving less than two days of rehearsal for the eight to twelve sketches that appear on the live broadcast.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show runtime constraint (90-minute review)
rubrics_metrics.description: After the rehearsal, Michaels reviews the show lineup to ensure it meets a 90-minute length; sketches that have made it as far as the live rehearsal may be removed to meet runtime.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The runtime constraint is a hard editorial filter late in the week and can result in material being cut even after live rehearsal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Opening monologue priority and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: The opening monologue, spoken by the guest host, is given low priority and can be written as late as Saturday afternoon.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Monologue may be developed after main sketches are finalized; its late timing reflects relative editorial priority compared with sketch material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Weekend Update writing and host collaboration
rubrics_metrics.description: A three- to four-member dedicated Weekend Update writing team writes jokes throughout the week. The host(s) of Weekend Update normally will not work with or read the team's scripts until Thursday evening after the main show sketches have been finalized.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hosts then contribute to the script where necessary; Weekend Update operates on a parallel but slightly offset schedule from main sketch development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Post-production mixing, element capture, and archiving
rubrics_metrics.description: Post-production duties include mixing of audio and video elements by the Senior Audio Mixer, adding additional audio feeds (music, sound effects, scoring, pre-recorded voiceovers), and storing all sources digitally with shows captured and segregated into individual elements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The production tracking system migrated from analog to digital in 1998; live shows typically require about 1.5 terabytes of storage consisting of audio elements and five cameras' worth of visual elements. Elements are organized for repeats and syndication.

rubrics_metrics.name: Processing of pre-recorded elements off-site
rubrics_metrics.description: Elements that are pre-recorded (commercial parodies, SNL Digital Shorts, show graphics) are processed off-site in the post-production facilities of Broadway Video.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Pre-recorded material is handled separately from live production facilities to allow different workflows and higher production values for filmed sketches.

rubrics_metrics.name: Studio production equipment and facility standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Studio 8H uses five Sony HDC-1500 cameras primarily mounted on Vinten pedestals (one on a Chapman-Leonard Electra crane); a Grass Valley GVG 4000-3 switcher and GVG 7000 router route visual feeds; graphics via Chyron Lyric Pro and Avid Deko; audio uses a Calrec T Series analog mixing console and a Yamaha digital mixing console.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These named camera, switching, graphics, and audio systems describe the technical baseline and interoperability expectations for live broadcast production at the facility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Broadcast timing and regulatory compliance
rubrics_metrics.description: The show begins at 11:29:30 p.m. Eastern and is scheduled for a 93-minute timeslot. Historically aired live only to Eastern and Central zones; since 2017 broadcast live across the contiguous United States. A brief broadcast delay is installed when airing outside of the safe harbor to meet Federal Communications Commission regulations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timing is coordinated to satisfy programming slots and FCC rules; coast-to-coast live broadcasting introduced additional use of broadcast delay to comply with regulations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling broadcast delays and contingency
rubrics_metrics.description: Episodes have been delayed or recorded later because of sports overruns (World Series, college football) or other scheduling conflicts; in some cases the show was recorded for the studio audience and broadcast weeks later.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Contingency includes recording for the studio audience and re-broadcasting at a later date; networks may negotiate feed cutoffs (e.g., sports feeds) to prevent future overruns impacting the scheduled start.

rubrics_metrics.name: International adaptations and format variations
rubrics_metrics.description: International versions have been created in many countries; adaptations vary — some copy the American format, others use original material; some versions are not broadcast live and some have different lengths (e.g., Japanese version was 45 minutes and hosted by a permanent host).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Local versions make format adjustments for language, broadcast norms, and production constraints; success varies and can include rebooting, changing networks, or cancellation for low ratings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Casting diversity and representation as an evaluative criterion
rubrics_metrics.description: SNL has been criticized for stereotypical and sparse representation of racial and gender groups (e.g., a 2016 study showed over 90% of episodes had white hosts; historically only eight Black female cast members), prompting critiques about inclusion and the value of varied perspectives.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Diversity metrics (host demographics, cast composition) are used by critics and researchers to evaluate the show's representativeness; producers have faced public pressure and internal debates about readiness and hiring practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Content risk and controversy management for live programming
rubrics_metrics.description: Because of its live broadcast, the show is subject to controversies involving controversial performers, profanities (intentional or accidental), technical problems, and accusations of joke plagiarism; incidents have led to hundreds of viewer complaints (e.g., Sinéad O'Connor ripping up a photo).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Live status requires risk awareness and sometimes last-minute editorial decisions or delays; historical incidents guide current content sensitivity and production safeguards.

rubrics_metrics.name: Rights, distribution, and syndication ownership
rubrics_metrics.description: NBC and Broadway Video hold underlying rights to the show, while copyrights to episodes lie with NBC or Universal Television; reruns and syndication agreements have varied across networks and streaming platforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Understanding rights ownership influences home media releases, DVD/streaming availability, and syndication deals; past distribution has included network reruns, cable channels, and streaming services.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotional photography scheduling and stylistic standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Photographers attempt to shoot the host on Tuesday and the musical guest on Thursday (though availability can force later shoots); portrait lighting uses hard lights to achieve a 'classic Hollywood' look providing contrast and depth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Limited turnaround times require makeshift on-site photo studios at 30 Rock; the photographic aesthetic (hard/edge lights, lit backgrounds) is applied consistently for bumpers and promotional imagery.
